newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing merger clears final EU hurdle.
newsitem.headline: Boeing merger clears final EU hurdle.

text.p: The European Commission, formally ending a five-month antitrust probe that brought Europe and the United States to the brink of a trade war, formally approved Wednesday Boeing Co.'s $16 billion acquisition of McDonnell Douglas Corp.

The decision by the Commission, the 15-nation European Union's executive body, was regarded as a formality after Boeing agreed last week to last-minute concessions that addressed EU concerns about the merger's impact on the civil aviation market.
EU national competition experts gave their blessing on Friday to the deal, which will form the world's largest aerospace company, expected to generate $49 billion in revenue this year.
"There was no vote. There was no discussion," an EU source said, referring to the meeting of the 20 European commissioners.
The Commission issued a statement declaring the merger compatible with the EU's common market, subject to Boeing's full compliance with the commitments it made.
"The EU merger regulation allows for appropriate measures to be taken by the Commission in the event of non-compliance by Boeing," the statement added.

To win EU approval, the Seattle-based aerospace giant pledged not to enforce exclusivity provisions in controversial long-term supply contracts with AMR Corp.'s American Airlines, Continental Airlines Inc. and Delta Air Lines Inc.

It also agreed not to strike any new supply contracts with airlines before August 2007, to keep McDonnell Douglas' commercial aircraft unit in a separate entity for 10 years and to license patents to other aircraft makers.

"These commitments are considered adequate to resolve the identified competition problems," the Commission said. It had earlier threatened to block the merger, saying it would strengthen Boeing's already dominant market position.

As a result of the merger, Boeing's share of the commercial jet market will increase to 70 percent from its current level of 64 percent, leaving only the European consortium Airbus Industrie in a position to compete.

The merger, which was announced in December and approved by the two companies' shareholders last Friday, also allows Boeing to reduce its dependence on the commercial aviation sector, as McDonnell Douglas mainly makes military aircraft.
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission unconditionally cleared the merger July 1.
